_: Bounds the compare table is held to. All three are absolute limits: 'median' caps the magnitude of the signed median, 'abs_median' caps the median absolute error, which is the one that can fail when errors of opposite sign cancel, and 'p90' caps the 90th percentile of that absolute error, which is the one that can fail when a minority of rows is far out and the median is not. A dimension can sit inside both medians while nearly half its rows are outside the references' own spread. 'rows' is how many of the grid's rows survived censoring into that median, so a later run can tell whether it is comparing against the same population. Re-record only in the same change as the behaviour that justifies it.

_unbounded.decay: the reference's usable decay span is 0.015-0.035 s, which is 3 to 7 points on the envelope's 5 ms hop and under the 9 `measure_note` needs to fit a slope, so `decay_db_s` is absent on 25 of 25 reference rows. Measured off the corpus, the reference falls 60 dB within 40 ms of its peak. The model's span is 0.060-0.065 s - it rings 1.86 to 4.33 times longer than the reference, and with no rate on the reference side nothing here holds that.
_unbounded.aftersound: as `decay`. `double_decay` needs 12 envelope points and the reference's span holds 3 to 7, so `decay_late_db_s` is absent on 25 of 25 reference rows.
_unbounded.doubling: as `decay`. `double_decay` never runs on the reference, so the prompt-minus-aftersound gap is absent on 25 of 25 reference rows and there is no pair to difference.
_unbounded.body: the 0.2-1.2 s body window opens 165 ms after the reference has already fallen 60 dB. Read off the corpus WAVs, that segment is exactly digital zero - absolute maximum 0.000e+00, RMS -240 dBFS - so both bands of `body_below_f0_db` are 0 and it returns nothing on 25 of 25 reference rows.
_unbounded.partial_tilt: as `decay`. Fitting a per-partial decay rate needs the same envelope points the free-fall slope does, so `partial_decay_db_s` is eight NaNs on 25 of 25 reference rows and there is no rate to split into high and low.
